tracks.title: The disk speaks SQL. Say what, exactly?
tracks.text: Lesson nine point one — queries. This one is a sub-lesson, under the VFS… the disk lesson. The parent page made a promise — your disk speaks SQL — and showed three dreamy queries, and left it there. That was the poetry. [curious] This page is the contract. If you are going to hand a SQL string to a component an LLM wrote, you want the answers underneath the slogan. What table… what columns… what exactly do I call… what comes back… and what happens when I get the query wrong. And the reassuring part is how small the truth is. There is no query API with a dozen methods. There is one table… one import… and one error shape. Once you have seen those three, you have seen all of it.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. vfs-query is the single, Policy-gated Dock import that runs one SQL string against the Instance's own disk… and returns JSON. Rows… or a caught error… and never a host crash. It is the working half of the VFS. That lesson described a disk you can query. This one names the exact seam the query passes through. One function… one string in… one string out. And the entire safety story rides on that narrow shape.

tracks.title: The whole schema, all of it
tracks.text: Next — the whole schema, all of it. Here is the disk, in full. Not an inode graph… not a manifest plus a blob store. One SQLite table, four columns, one file per Instance. Let me read you the table. It is named vfs. Column one… volume… a text field that names the region. Column two… path… a text field, the file name within that volume. Column three… content… the raw bytes, one row per file. And column four… mtime… an integer, unix seconds, written on every save. The primary key is volume and path together — so a path is unique within a volume. That is one hundred percent of the schema. [excited] You have now seen the whole grammar. Now the reconciliation the parent owes you. It drew queries against a files table — with size, and dir, and writer columns. None of those columns exist. Size is the length of the content. A directory is a string operation on the path. And writer attribution simply is not in the schema at all — there is no column that records who wrote a row. So the parent's query — select path from files where mtime is after June ninth — told truthfully, becomes this. Select path, and length of content as bytes, from vfs, where volume equals workspace, and mtime is greater than the unix seconds for June ninth. And the result comes back like this — an array holding two arrays. First… slash reports slash week twenty-four dot org, eighteen thousand two hundred thirty-four bytes. Second… slash notes slash june dot org, four thousand one hundred one bytes. Carry two things out of that. First — rows come back as arrays of arrays, not objects with named keys. Second — the size you wanted was derived, not stored. Four columns is the whole grammar. Everything else is SQL you already know.

tracks.title: One import, granted or absent
tracks.text: One import — granted, or absent. There is exactly one way in. The engine declares it as a single typed function — import vfs-query, a function taking a SQL string and returning a string. A string in… a string out. But a component does not always have that import. It has it only if its Policy profile grants the vfs capability. When the host assembles a component's imports, granting vfs adds precisely one entry to the map — vfs-query — bound to a closure over this Instance's own database connection. No grant… no entry. And here is the part that makes the gating airtight — it is gating by construction, not by a runtime check. Picture a flowchart, top to bottom, as one sentence. At the top… a Policy profile. It names a caps list. The caps list either contains vfs… or it does not. If it does, one import appears in the map, and the component links cleanly to its own disk — that branch ends in green, instantiated. If it does not, the component asking for that import never finishes loading — that branch ends in the failed state. [curious] So a component that imports vfs-query without the grant does not get an error when it calls. It fails to instantiate. An unauthorized capability is a wire that was never run. Two endpoints… and which one you reach was decided before a line of the component ran.

tracks.title: The round trip
tracks.text: Now follow one call — the round trip. Picture a sequence, four participants. The component… the Dock import… the host function query-json… and SQLite, this Instance's disk. The component speaks the SDK's ergonomic surface — in Rust, vfs query of a type; in JavaScript, dock dot vfs dot query. Watch the message travel. First, the component calls query — select path from vfs where volume equals memory. Second, the Dock import passes that raw string through to query-json on the host. Third, the host prepares the statement and fetches every row from the single SQLite file that is this Instance's disk. Fourth, the rows come back as plain lists… get encoded into one JSON string… and ride home across the same boundary, where the SDK parses them into the array of arrays the component reads. One string out… one string back. [curious] The boundary never carries anything richer than text. Which is exactly what makes the next part possible.

tracks.title: Error as a value
tracks.text: Error as a value — and crash as an impossibility. Hand SQL to a component an LLM wrote… and it will get a query wrong. A typo… a missing table… a malformed clause. The host treats your SQL as untrusted by default, and the design line is blunt — the Instance must not be able to take down its engine. So the host wraps the query, and on failure it does not trap. It returns an error envelope down the very same string channel as the rows. Let me read you both shapes. The good case is a JSON array of row arrays — for example, one array holding the path slash notes slash june dot org and a timestamp. The bad case is an object with one key, exactly — error — mapping to the string near quote SELEC… syntax error. Picture the flowchart. Prepare and fetch on the left. A branch — ok? If yes… rows JSON, in green. If no… error JSON, in amber. And both arrows rejoin into one wire — the single return-string wire back to the component. [excited] Both outcomes leave by the same door. There is no second channel for errors, no exception that crosses the boundary. The component decides which it got by looking at the shape — and both SDKs sniff for exactly that one-key envelope and raise it as a typed error. Now one honest nuance, because it matters. The design describes this as a read query… but nothing mechanically rejects a write. An insert or a delete will happily run. The guarantee is not statement-kind. It is scope. The only bytes that SQL can touch are this Instance's own disk. The blast radius of the worst query you can write… is one project-sized file.

tracks.title: Who holds the cap
tracks.text: A depth rung — who holds the cap. Skippable. The vfs capability is the floor. Every Policy profile grants it. The only thing that changes, profile to profile, is what else comes with it… and how much memory and time the component gets. Picture four profiles. First… compute — the true sandbox — vfs only, nothing more, sixty-four mebibytes, a five second timeout. Second… minimal — vfs plus the local caps and raw sockets, same sixty-four megs, five seconds — so for a true sandbox, reach for compute, not minimal. Third… network — vfs plus net, one hundred twenty-eight megs, thirty seconds. And fourth… posix — vfs and more, two hundred fifty-six megs, sixty seconds. The verdict in one line — vfs is in every row, so the query surface is always available… but it is the floor, never the ceiling. And the fail-safe points the right way. A typo'd or unknown profile fails closed… to compute… the vfs-only sandbox. Never up to something more permissive. So a runaway query ends as a clean cpu-timeout… not a hung engine.

tracks.title: One statement, a whole shelf
tracks.text: One statement… a whole shelf. Here is the payoff of one table per disk. Because every workbook's disk is the same four-column SQLite file, asking a question of your whole library needs no new query engine at all. The library query takes one SQL statement and runs it across every member that is a bundle. And a bundle is just a plain zip of the workbook HTML, a vfs sqlite file, and a manifest — so its disk is right there to read. Picture the fan-out. One SQL statement at the top, going out to three members. First member… weekly-orders, a bundle. Its vfs sqlite gets restored to its own throwaway temp copy, the statement runs, and the rows come back tagged with which member and which workspace — then merge into one result. Second member… wulu, also a bundle, same path, restored and queried and merged. Third member… press-kit — HTML only, no disk to query. It takes the one branch to the side, into skipped — listed, never lost. And the stored bundles are never mutated — each one is queried on a throwaway temp copy that gets deleted. Let me read you a real run. You type wbx library query… select path from vfs where volume equals workspace and path begins with slash reports. And back comes an object. Rows holds two entries. weekly-orders, workspace ops, with one row — slash reports slash week twenty-four dot org. And wulu, workspace sites, with an empty rows list — it is a bundle, it answered, it just had no match. And then skipped — holding press-kit. [excited] press-kit is HTML only, so it shows up in skipped rather than vanishing. The same query is reachable over HTTP — a POST to slash api slash library, with a body holding the sql. The surface is the CLI, the API, or the host directly. The engine underneath… is the one you already learned.

tracks.title: When FROM isn't a file
tracks.text: A depth rung — when FROM is not a file. Skippable. One thing sits in front of the library sweep. Before fanning a statement out over members' disks, the library query checks whether the table named in the FROM clause is a registered data source. If it is, federation answers the query through a plugin instead, and the result is tagged federated. If it is not — not-federated — the query falls through to the per-member VFS sweep you just saw. So the same entry point serves both a question about your files and a question about a foreign table… and the routing decides which, without you choosing a different verb. The depth of that — what a data source is, how a plugin answers — belongs to the foreign-tables lesson. Here it is enough to know the fork exists… and which branch the file-sweep is.

tracks.title: Where the query ends
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the query ends. Five edges, named plainly. First — rows are arrays, not named objects. The host returns lists in column order, not dictionaries with keys. If you saw an object-shaped fixture in a test, that was a stub, not host output. Bind your results by position. Second — there is no writer column. Who wrote a file is not recorded anywhere in the schema. The parent's writer-equals-agent query was illustrative — you cannot run it, because the fact it queries does not exist. Third — read-query is intent, not mechanism. Nothing rejects an insert or a delete. The guarantee is scope — your own disk — not statement-kind. Fourth — vfs-query is not in the step log. The Dock logs run-command calls into a steps file… but vfs-query calls are not logged the same way. An honest asymmetry, not a hidden audit trail. And fifth — the library sweep is linear. It restores and scans each member's disk in turn. Lovely for a shelf… not a search engine for ten thousand bundles.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can a bad query crash the engine? No. A syntax error comes back as an error envelope, the same string channel as rows. The Instance cannot trap its host with a query. Can the SQL write, not just read? Yes — and that is the point, not a leak. An insert or a delete will run, but the only disk it can touch is this Instance's own. The worst a write can do is rearrange one project-sized file. Why arrays instead of named objects? Because the host returns rows as plain lists and encodes them straight to JSON. Bind your columns by position. Can I query another workbook's memory volume? No. When a bundle ships, only the public volume goes with it — memory and tmp are stripped on egress. And is there a query budget? Yes — the profile's wall-clock timeout. A runaway query ends as a clean cpu-timeout, not a hung engine.

tracks.title: Back up to the VFS
tracks.text: So that is queries. One four-column table… one Policy-gated import… one error envelope that turns a broken query into a value instead of a crash. And because every disk is the same file, one statement can sweep a whole shelf. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This sub-lesson stands on one parent — the VFS, lesson nine — the disk this whole page queries. Go meet the disk… and then come back and ask it a question.
